questions.q: In this chapter's lab, why was the resource group tagged with environment, costcenter, and owner before any VM or storage account existed?
options: Tags were added only after the cost spike in Lesson 31 was discovered
Because az vm create fails if its resource group has no tags
Because tags determine which Azure region a resource group can use
Because governance is meant to be the container everything else is built inside, not something added after resources already exist
questions.explain: Chapter 1's governance argument is that structure like tags belongs at the start, which is exactly how Lesson 29 built it — and exactly what Lesson 31's investigation later relied on.

questions.q: What do this chapter's VM sizing (Standard_B2s) and storage tier (Standard_LRS) choices have in common with the cost spike in Lesson 31?
options: Right-sizing only applies to storage accounts, never to virtual machines
Standard_B2s and Standard_LRS were the resources responsible for the cost spike
They have no relationship; sizing and storage tiers are unrelated to the cost spike's cause
Both are examples of right-sizing — matching the resource tier to the actual workload — which is exactly the discipline that failed with loadtest-vm1 and its Premium_LRS disk
questions.explain: Lesson 31's incident was the same right-sizing discipline failing once — an oversized VM and an oversized disk tier left running for a workload that didn't need either.

questions.q: How does app-nsg's rule set connect Chapter 5's subnetting concept to its security-rule concept in this chapter's lab?
options: app-nsg allows traffic from the internet directly, bypassing the subnet structure entirely
NSG rules apply at the virtual-network level only, never at the subnet level
Splitting the VNet into web-subnet and app-subnet gave the NSG rules something meaningful to attach to, so app-nsg could allow traffic only from web-subnet's address range
Subnetting and NSG rules are handled by two completely separate Azure services with no relationship to each other
questions.explain: The two-subnet layout from Lesson 29 is what made it possible for app-nsg to scope its allow rule specifically to the web subnet's own address range in Lesson 30.

questions.q: According to this review, what was Chapter 6's real role across the whole course, beyond its own four lessons?
options: Chapter 6's commands were only used in Lesson 29, not in any other lesson of this chapter
Chapter 6 replaced the need to learn the Azure Portal for any task in this course
The az CLI it taught became the thread running through every other chapter's commands — governance, identity, compute, storage, networking, and monitoring all expressed as az commands
Chapter 6 was a standalone topic with no connection to any other chapter's material
questions.explain: Every command used across Lessons 29-31 — az group create, az role assignment create, az vm create, az network nsg rule create, az monitor metrics alert create, and more — is a direct application of Chapter 6's CLI skills.

questions.q: What distinguishes an environment that is merely 'deployed' from one that is 'operated,' as this chapter uses the terms?
options: An operated environment no longer has any resource group or tags
There is no real difference — both terms describe the same thing in Azure
An operated environment has monitoring and cost alerts in place that catch problems automatically, like the budget alert that opened Lesson 31's investigation
An operated environment uses more expensive VM sizes than a deployed one
questions.explain: Chapter 7's monitoring and cost alerts are what turn a one-time deployment into something actually watched and operated, which is exactly how Lesson 31's cost spike got caught on day 19 instead of at month-end.
